prize_parts.citation: For foundational contributions to the analysis of nominal rigidities and monetary policy: time-dependent price setting, staggered contracts with interest-rate policy rules, and the microfounded, welfare-based theory of optimal monetary policy.

statement.case_for: My configuration is unchanged from round 1: B014, credited to Calvo, Taylor and Woodford. The exchange did not alter the names. It sharpened how the citation should be worded and how far it can claim to reach. The case rests on originality, breadth and durability. Calvo's time-dependent pricing is the tractable primitive of the microfounded Phillips curve. Taylor's staggered contracts and policy rule gave systematic policy a simple, testable and communicable benchmark. Woodford's welfare-based synthesis turned the pieces into a coherent theory of interest rates, prices and optimal policy. These are three separable, load-bearing contributions, each identifiable in a specific body of work, and the framework has been taught, estimated and used in central banks for 25 to 40 years. The 2008 crisis, the zero lower bound and the 2021-23 inflation have produced extensions such as financial frictions and heterogeneous agents, not abandonment. That reads to me as foundational status, though I accept the evidence admits the other reading. Six explicit round-1 preferences for B014 equal the majority threshold, but I do not treat that count as merit, and my own preference rests on the criteria above. Of the main rivals, B003 has the cleaner attribution but a narrower footprint, and B047 has a clean pair but a harder priority problem. Neither displaces B014 once breadth of influence on scientific practice and on policy is weighed alongside attribution. The citation names the three components and does not claim the estimated-DSGE tradition. That answers the chair's scope question as well as a three-person cap can.
statement.case_against: Attribution remains the strongest reservation. Christiano, Eichenbaum and Evans (identification of monetary shocks and the medium-scale model), Smets and Wouters, Galí and Gertler all made major contributions, and the cap excludes people whose work made the framework empirically usable. No wording removes that cost. It can only avoid asserting that these contributions are derivative. Second, the performance of the representative-agent framework in 2008 and 2021-23 is contested, and a prize could be read as rewarding a stage of development that heterogeneous-agent work is superseding. Third, one can ask whether Calvo's compact pricing device is a discovery in the sense the Committee usually rewards, rather than a modelling convenience that became ubiquitous. Fourth, B003 is a cleaner two-person case. If the Committee puts attribution clarity and marginal distinctiveness above breadth of influence, B003 is a legitimate winner. I would not call that outcome an error.

responses.point: Strömberg says he would support B014 if a defensible, narrower citation or attribution were found. He argues that Calvo's pricing, Taylor's contracts and rule, and Woodford's synthesis are different discoveries, so the citation must say which it rewards. He still sees B003 as the cleaner prize.
responses.response: I think the citation can meet his condition by crediting the three components explicitly and making no claim to the whole field. My wording is: time-dependent price setting, staggered contracts with interest-rate rules, and the microfounded welfare-based theory of optimal policy. It says what each name is credited for and leaves the estimated-DSGE tradition unmentioned, so it does not imply the omitted contributors are lesser. Whether that suffices is his call. I agree B003's attribution is cleaner and I keep it as my first alternative. I part from him on whether attribution should decide the matter. It is one criterion, and I give more weight to the breadth with which B014 changed both research practice and policy conduct. He concedes that B014 has the larger footprint in practice.

responses.point: Hjalmarsson keeps Calvo over Galí because Calvo's pricing mechanism is the primitive of the New Keynesian Phillips curve. She would not object strongly to Galí in place of Calvo if the Committee weighted the estimated-model tradition more heavily.
responses.response: I agree on the structure of the contributions and would add a point about the swap. A citation weighted toward the empirical and estimated framework becomes less stable, not more. Once the empirical weight is applied, the claim of Christiano, Eichenbaum and Evans, and of Smets and Wouters, is at least as strong as Galí's, and a three-person cap cannot honour it. A conceptual citation built on the pricing friction, the rule and the synthesis has a coherent internal logic and does not hand an advantage to a particular excluded claimant. So Galí for Calvo is a defensible alternative, but I think it solves the attribution problem less well than it appears to. I keep Calvo.

responses.point: Boppart ranks B047 first and B014 second. His objection to B014 is that a trio cannot carry the discovery. He notes that Calvo's and Taylor's older contract-pricing and rule insights differ from the Woodford-Galí synthesis, so the Committee must say what it is crediting. He also records the tension with the framework's performance in 2008 and 2021-22.
responses.response: The citation question is fair, and my answer is that the prize credits the pricing friction, the rule and the synthesis as three components of one framework, not a single discovery. Woodford carries the synthesis, and Galí's Phillips-curve work is best read as a development within it, so I do not need a fourth name to credit that layer. I accept that this is a conceptual award, and I accept your point that its attribution is more contestable than Melitz-Helpman. I do not accept that B047's attribution is clean once the priority of Bernard, Eaton, Jensen and Kortum is counted, and your own uncertainty list admits that. On performance, my view is unchanged. The prize rewards originality and influence on how the field analyses questions, not predictive success in particular episodes. The framework was revised after both episodes.

responses.point: Fredriksson moved from Woodford, Galí and Taylor to Calvo, Taylor and Woodford, and wants the citation worded so it does not claim to cover the estimated DSGE tradition. He asks whether Calvo's compact device is a discovery in the sense the Committee normally rewards.
responses.response: I agree on the wording. The proposed citation is built to leave the estimated tradition unclaimed. On whether Calvo's device counts as a discovery, I think it does. A tractable representation that makes forward-looking pricing analysable changed what models could be built and what questions could be asked, and nearly every later New Keynesian derivation inherits it. Size alone should not disqualify a contribution, and the Committee has credited compact devices before when their consequences were large. I accept that this is a judgement and not a demonstration, and I list it as an open uncertainty.

responses.point: Hassler (chair) moved from B030 to B014 and now holds Calvo, Taylor and Woodford. He keeps B006 fourth because of the density of recent game-theory prizes in 2005, 2007, 2012 and 2020, and he says he would weigh that as a narrowing of marginal contribution, not as a verdict on quality.
responses.response: I agree with the distinction between marginal contribution and quality, and it is the reason B006 stays an alternative. In round 1 I told him that alternating-offers bargaining was not itself covered by those prizes. I still think so, but I weigh the narrower reach beyond theory more heavily than I did in my opening. I also note that the chair and I now name the same trio, and that shared co-authorship ties among several B014 supporters are disclosed in his summary. I try to guard against reading agreement as evidence. My own view has three separate supports: the distinct contributions, the decades of testing, and the breadth of use.

uncertainties: Whether Calvo or Galí is the right third name. I judge Calvo's claim more clearly originating, but a Committee that weights the empirical framework heavily could reasonably choose otherwise, and that choice would favour Christiano, Eichenbaum and Evans more than it favours Galí.

Whether a three-person conceptual citation can avoid implying a ranking against Christiano, Eichenbaum, Evans, Smets, Wouters and Gertler. I think the wording avoids asserting it, but a reader may infer it anyway.
How much the post-2021 inflation and the heterogeneous-agent critique should weigh on maturity. I read them as extension, but I cannot name an observation that would settle the matter.

How to apply a consistent standard to prior-prize overlap: 2022 for B003, 2008 for B047 and B030, 2024 for B032, and the game-theory prizes for B006. My own application may be coloured by my adjacency to B006.

Whether B003 should outrank B014 if the Committee treats attribution clarity and marginal distinctiveness as the decisive criteria. That would be a legitimate ordering, and it is the main way my preferred outcome could fail.
I have not independently verified priority and attribution claims from outside the supplied evidence.
statement.conflict_note: None apparent from the supplied profile for Calvo, Taylor or Woodford, or for the other B014 names. The profile lists no co-authorship or institutional link with them. My field is microeconomic theory and market design, which is adjacent to B006 (Rubinstein, Wolinsky). That is an alternative only, and I note the proximity as a possible familiarity bias, not a recusal-level connection. I am a Lund colleague of Kerstin Enflo and an SSE affiliate alongside committee members Dreber Almenberg, Friberg and Strömberg. These are ties to colleagues, not to candidates. Conflicts are disclosed, not adjudicated.
